title: India Rolls Out First Export-Grade Shipping Container, Challenging China's 95% Grip
excerpt: DCM Shriram Group delivered the first EXIM-certified container to Maersk at Dadri, Uttar Pradesh, backed by a ₹10,000 crore government scheme to build domestic manufacturing capacity tenfold.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • India launched its first export-grade shipping container, manufactured by DCM Shriram Group.
  • Maersk ordered 1,000 additional containers, marking a shift from prototype to procurement.
  • The government allocated ₹10,000 crore to boost container manufacturing capacity tenfold by 2026.
  • Indian containers are 30-40% more expensive than Chinese ones, prompting government support to close the gap.

On July 3, 2026, Union Minister Sarbananda Sonowal flagged off the first export-import grade container manufactured in India for an international shipping line. The steel box, built by DCM Shriram Group at its Faridabad facility, was handed over to A.P. Moller-Maersk — the world's second-largest shipping line — at Container Corp. of India's inland container depot in Dadri, Uttar Pradesh.

The event carried a significance out of proportion to a single steel box. Chinese manufacturers produce more than 95% of the world's dry cargo containers and close to 100% of refrigerated ones, according to shipping consultancy Drewry. CIMC alone accounts for roughly 42-45% of global production, with Dong Fang and CXIC taking most of the rest. In May 2026, the US Justice Department unsealed an indictment against four Chinese container makers and seven executives for allegedly running a price-fixing cartel that roughly doubled prices between 2019 and 2021.

From Prototype to Procurement

India has had container capacity before — Jupiter Wagons operates a plant in Indore — but what distinguishes this milestone is certification. The DCM Shriram container meets ISO structural and dimensional specifications, the International Convention for Safe Containers, and Maersk's own elevated internal quality standards, according to the ministry of ports, shipping and waterways. Structural prototype testing, including stacking, lifting, racking, floor strength, and weatherproofing, was conducted under a classification society's oversight.

"This is Atmanirbhar Bharat in action, and I am delighted that Maersk has chosen to lead from the front."

— Sarbananda Sonowal, Union Minister for Ports, Shipping and Waterways

Maersk ordering 1,000 more India-made containers immediately after the unveiling is small by global standards — carriers buy tens of thousands a year — but meaningful as a first repeat purchase that moves a supplier from prototype to commercial procurement. The milestone came 16 months after Prime Minister Narendra Modi met Maersk chairman Robert Maersk Uggla in February 2025, according to Mint.

The Cost Gap and the Subsidy Bridge

China's dominance didn't happen by accident. Production migrated from the US to Japan to South Korea — which by the 1980s built more than 70% of the world's containers — before Chinese scale, cheap steel, and state support made competing elsewhere unworkable.

The barrier remains cost, not physics. A 40-foot container costs roughly ₹1.5-2 lakh to build in China versus ₹3.5-4 lakh in India, according to YourStory — a 30-40% premium that translates to $700-$1,000 per unit. Indian producers face higher land costs, smaller production volumes, and lower levels of automation compared to Chinese factories, Outlook Business reported.

The Union Budget 2026 allocated ₹10,000 crore over five years to bridge that gap through the Container Manufacturing Promotion Scheme (CMPS). The programme aims to lift annual capacity tenfold, from roughly 30,000 TEUs to 7.5 lakh TEUs, through capital support for new plants, operating incentives to offset production costs, and R&D funding. The government is targeting ₹60,000 crore in total investment to build large-scale capacity, with interest from global shipping giants including MSC and CMA CGM alongside domestic firms like JSW Group.

Vietnam Shows the Path — and the Challenge

India isn't the first challenger. Vietnam's Hoa Phat built a container plant beside its own steel mill in Vung Tau and delivered 1,000 twenty-foot boxes to CMA CGM in August 2025. It now runs 200,000 TEUs a year of a designed 500,000 TEU capacity. That example cuts both ways: the monopoly is contestable, but contesting it demands captive steel supply, proximity to export markets, and patience.

The real test, as YourStory noted, is whether DCM Shriram can deliver repeat quality at a cost that survives the eventual withdrawal of subsidies. India's current domestic capacity of 30,000 TEUs against China's six million annually underscores the scale of the ambition.

The container push fits within a broader maritime self-reliance strategy. The government has announced a ₹70,000 crore financial assistance package for shipbuilding, is investing in major port infrastructure including the Vadhavan Port in Maharashtra and the Galathea Bay transshipment port in the Andaman and Nicobar Islands, and is working on plans for a national container shipping line.

For India's exporters, reducing dependence on Chinese-made containers addresses a vulnerability exposed during Covid-19, when container shortages and soaring freight rates disrupted supply chains globally. One box won't dent China's dominance, but it is a genuine entry into a market that has had almost no alternatives for over a decade.

nri_angle: Reduced container costs and supply chain resilience would benefit Indian exporters and lower trade disruption risk for diaspora businesses engaged in India-linked commerce.
